_meta.note: anchor_date is the fixed 'today' baked into db/seed.py for relative-date questions (e.g. 'last quarter'). All expected_result values were produced by running canonical_sql against db/guardrails.db, not hand-computed.

questions.question: List the names and states of all customers in California.
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT name, state FROM customers WHERE state = 'CA' ORDER BY customer_id
questions.expected_result_note: 58 rows total; sample shown, full result reproducible by re-running canonical_sql.

questions.question: What is Jordan Blake's email address and signup date?
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT email, signup_date FROM customers WHERE name = 'Jordan Blake'

questions.question: Which products are in the 'Hardware' category, and what do they cost?
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE category = 'Hardware'

questions.question: List all subscriptions for the customer with email avery.nguyen@example.com.
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT plan_name, subscription_start_date, status FROM subscriptions s JOIN customers c ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE c.email = 'avery.nguyen@example.com'

questions.question: How many enterprise-tier customers signed up in Q2 2025 (Apr 1 - Jun 30)?
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE tier = 'enterprise' AND signup_date BETWEEN '2025-04-01' AND '2025-06-30'

questions.question: What is the total dollar amount of successful payments in 2024?
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded' AND payment_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'
questions.notes: Trap: 'payments' includes both order payments and subscription renewal payments, and both failed and refunded rows exist alongside succeeded ones. A query that forgets status='succeeded' or sums all payments regardless of type will overstate this.

questions.question: How many customers are on the 'basic' tier?
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE tier = 'basic'

questions.question: What is the average order amount for completed orders?
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT ROUND(AVG(amount), 2) FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed'
questions.notes: Trap: omitting status='completed' pulls in pending/refunded orders and changes the average.

questions.question: How many subscriptions are currently active?
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM subscriptions WHERE status = 'active'
questions.notes: 'Currently' means as of anchor_date (2025-07-01), which is how status was assigned in the seed data. Equivalent to COUNT(*) WHERE end_date IS NULL in this dataset.

questions.question: What is the total revenue by product category, counting only completed orders?
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT p.category, ROUND(SUM(o.amount), 2) AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id WHERE o.status = 'completed' GROUP BY p.category ORDER BY revenue DESC

questions.question: List the names of customers who have at least one refunded order.
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'refunded' ORDER BY c.name

questions.question: How many subscription-renewal payments failed for enterprise-tier customers?
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payments pay JOIN subscriptions s ON pay.subscription_id = s.subscription_id JOIN customers c ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE c.tier = 'enterprise' AND pay.status = 'failed'
questions.notes: Three-table join (payments -> subscriptions -> customers). Trap: payments.subscription_id is NULL for order-linked payments, so a naive join without the subscription_id path (or one that joins via orders instead) silently drops or double counts rows.

questions.question: What is the total amount spent on 'Service' category products by pro-tier customers, for completed orders?
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT ROUND(SUM(o.amount), 2) FROM orders o JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE p.category = 'Service' AND c.tier = 'pro' AND o.status = 'completed'

questions.question: List the names of customers who have placed more than 3 orders.
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS n_orders FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) > 3 ORDER BY c.name
questions.expected_result_note: 36 rows, all with n_orders = 4 (the max in this dataset). Full result reproducible by re-running canonical_sql.
questions.notes: Two customers share the display name 'Rowan Fischer' (different customer_id) -- a name-based lookup elsewhere would be ambiguous; this query correctly groups by customer_id.

questions.question: What was our revenue last month?
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded' AND payment_date BETWEEN '2025-06-01' AND '2025-06-30'
questions.notes: Genuinely ambiguous, no single correct answer: (1) 'last month' has no year and depends entirely on an undefined 'now' -- the canonical_sql assumes anchor_date 2025-07-01 as 'now', so 'last month' = June 2025; (2) 'revenue' could mean succeeded payments only (used here), all payment attempts regardless of status, or orders.amount for completed orders -- these give different numbers. This question exists to test whether Layer 4 flags low confidence rather than to be answered 'correctly'.

questions.question: Who are our best customers?
questions.notes: No canonical SQL -- 'best' is undefined. Could mean highest lifetime spend, longest tenure, highest tier, most orders, or highest-value active subscription, and each produces a different customer list. Exists to test whether the model asks for clarification / flags uncertainty instead of confidently picking one interpretation.

questions.question: What is the total amount charged for order #4?
questions.canonical_sql: SELECT amount FROM orders WHERE order_id = 4
questions.notes: Not ambiguous in principle -- there is one correct answer (41.65, matching orders.amount) -- but it is a trap for a plausible-looking wrong query. Order 4 has two payment rows: a 'failed' attempt and the 'succeeded' retry, both for 41.65. A query that instead computes SUM(amount) FROM payments WHERE order_id=4 returns 83.30, silently double-counting the failed attempt. This is the exact 'amount exists on both orders and payments' trap called out in Layer 0.

questions.question: How many customers signed up recently?
questions.notes: No canonical SQL -- 'recently' is undefined (last week? last month? last quarter?) and no reference date is given. Exists to test whether the model guesses a silent default window instead of surfacing the ambiguity.
